content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Plot scatter graphs from paired data
Identify positive, negative, and no correlation
Scatter graphs (also called scatter diagrams or scatter plots) are used to investigate the
between two variables. For example, is there a link between hours of revision and exam score? Or between temperature and ice cream sales?
Unlike bar charts and pie charts which display one variable, scatter graphs plot
of data to look for patterns.
Explore scatter graphs — plot data points and describe the correlation using the interactive visualisation below.
Points are plotted as crosses ($\times$) or dots
As one variable increases, the other also increases.
Points slope upward from left to right
As one variable increases, the other decreases.
Example: Price of a car and its age
Points slope downward from left to right
There is no clear relationship between the variables.
Points lie close to a straight line.
Points show a general trend but are widely scattered.
is a point that does not fit the general pattern. It lies far from the other points or from the line of best fit.
Just because two variables are correlated does not mean one causes the other.
Example: Ice cream sales and drowning incidents are positively correlated -- but ice cream does not cause drowning. Both are caused by a third factor: hot weather.
The table shows hours of revision and test scores for 8 students.
Plotting these points shows that as hours of revision increase, the test score also increases. The points lie fairly close to a straight line.
. Students who revised more tended to score higher on the test.
The table shows the age and value of 7 used cars.
Describe the relationship between age and value.
As the age of the car increases, its value decreases. The points lie close to a straight line sloping downward.
. Older cars tend to be worth less.
The scatter graph below shows the relationship between the temperature and the number of hot drinks sold.
(a) Describe the correlation. (b) One day had a temperature of $12°$C and 42 hot drinks were sold. Is this point an outlier?
. As temperature increases, the number of hot drinks sold decreases.

(b) At $12°$C, the general pattern suggests about 33--35 drinks sold. A value of 42 is somewhat higher than expected but is close to the trend. It could be a minor outlier or within normal variation -- it depends on how far it is from the line of best fit. If it lies significantly away from the trend, it would be considered an outlier.
A student finds a positive correlation between the number of fire engines sent to a fire and the damage caused. She concludes that "fire engines cause damage." Explain why this conclusion is wrong.
Correlation does not imply causation. The real reason for the positive correlation is a
: the size of the fire. Bigger fires cause more damage AND require more fire engines. The fire engines do not cause the damage -- the fire does.

Plot points as crosses; do not join them

Identify outliers and consider their effect
